problems.title: Cache per thread
problems.statement: Divide cache capacity by the threads that share it.

parts.prompt: 256 KB of L1 per SM over 2,048 resident threads: bytes per thread?
The GW-1's 256 KB L2 over all its threads (16 SMs × 2,048)?

problems.solution: (a) 128 bytes, about one cache line. (b) 8 bytes: two floats. GPU caches work through sharing between neighbouring threads, not private working sets.

problems.title: Cyclic sweeps and LRU
problems.statement: A kernel sweeps an array repeatedly, in the same order, through the GW-1's 256 KB LRU L2. No other traffic.

parts.prompt: Hit rate on the second and later passes for a 192 KB array, in %?
For a 320 KB array, in %?

hints: LRU evicts the least recently used sector; in a cyclic sweep that's the one needed next.
problems.solution: (a) It fits: 100%. (b) Each sector is evicted just before it's needed again: 0%. LRU has a cliff for cyclic access just past capacity; a 25% bigger working set loses all reuse.

problems.title: L2-bound or DRAM-bound?
problems.statement: A kernel moves 400 MB between the SMs and L2 with a 60% L2 hit rate. L2 bandwidth 1,024 GB/s, DRAM 512 GB/s.

parts.prompt: DRAM traffic, in MB?
Lower bound on time, in ms?
Which level limits it?

hints: Time bound = max(L2 bytes / L2 bw, DRAM bytes / DRAM bw).
problems.solution: (a) 40% of 400 MB = 160 MB. (b) $\max(0.391, 0.3125) = 0.391$ ms. (c) L2. A high hit rate shifts the bottleneck up the hierarchy.

problems.title: Walking columns
problems.statement: A loop walks down column c of an N × N row-major float matrix (one element per row), then down column c + 1, and so on. Each access touches the 32-byte sector holding (row, c), which also holds 7 neighbouring columns. The only traffic goes through the GW-1's 256 KB LRU L2.

parts.prompt: Bytes of distinct sectors touched by one column walk, for N = 4096, in KB?
For N = 4096: how many times is each sector fetched from DRAM?

hints: The reuse distance between (row, c) and (row, c + 1) is one whole column walk.
Does N sectors fit in 256 KB?
problems.solution: (a) 4,096 sectors × 32 bytes = 128 KB. (b) That fits, so when column c + 1 comes back to the same sectors they're still cached: each is fetched once and used 8 times. (c) 16,384 sectors = 512 KB doesn't fit; LRU evicts each sector before its next use, so it's fetched 8 times, once per column it holds: 8× the necessary DRAM traffic. The fix is to walk a strip of 8 (or 32) columns together, so each sector is fully used while it's in cache: a reuse-distance fix, not a bandwidth one.

problems.title: Repeated GEMV
problems.statement: Ten iterations of $y = Ax$ with the same A (FP32), in a 256 KB L2.

parts.prompt: A is 128 × 256 (128 KB): DRAM bytes for A over the 10 iterations?

problems.solution: (a) Fits: A comes from DRAM once, 128 KB; the next nine passes hit. (b) Doesn't fit and is swept cyclically: 40 MB. Small operators reused across iterations (or kernels) can live in L2; Ampere's persisting-L2 controls make that deliberate.

problems.title: Restructuring for LRU
problems.statement: A kernel makes 10 passes over a 512 KB array through a 256 KB LRU cache.

parts.prompt: Overall hit rate as written (10 full sweeps), in %?
Restructured: 10 passes over the first half, then 10 over the second half. Hit rate, in %?

hints: Only the first pass over each half misses.
problems.solution: (a) 0%: the cyclic-sweep cliff. (b) Each 256 KB half misses on its first pass and hits on the other nine: 90%. This is loop tiling for caches: reorder work so that reuse happens within a working set that fits.

problems.title: Where writes go

parts.prompt: On most NVIDIA GPUs, global stores…
options: are cached in L1 and written back on eviction
go to L2, where they're merged; L1 isn't used for them
bypass every cache and go straight to DRAM

problems.solution: Stores go to L2 (writes from different SMs to the same line must meet somewhere coherent). In the simulator a written sector that misses L2 counts as one sector of DRAM traffic.

problems.title: A large table, random lookups
problems.statement: An embedding table of 4 MB is read at uniformly random rows through a 2 MB LRU cache, 1M lookups of 32 bytes each, after warm-up.

parts.prompt: Expected hit rate, in %?
DRAM bytes for the 1M lookups, in MB (10⁶ bytes)?

hints: Under uniform random access, the cache holds a random half of the table.
problems.solution: (a) About $2/4 = 50\%$. (b) Half of 32 MB: 16 MB. For random access, hit rate ≈ capacity / working set; only shrinking the table (compression, smaller types) or reordering lookups helps.

problems.title: The three Cs
problems.statement: Classify misses in the simulator's fully associative LRU L2.

parts.prompt: Which kinds of miss can happen in a fully associative LRU cache?
options: Conflict: too many lines mapping to one set

parts.prompt: A kernel reads a 64 MB array once. Its misses are…

problems.solution: (a) Fully associative caches have no sets, so no conflict misses: only compulsory and capacity. Real GPU caches are set-associative and do have conflict misses. (b) A single pass: every miss is a first touch.

problems.title: Neighbour reuse in a blur
problems.statement: A 5-tap horizontal blur on a 512 × 512 float image; warps go left to right along rows. Count DRAM bytes per pixel.

parts.prompt: If every read went to DRAM (no caching)?
With the cache serving all repeats?
Reuse distance of a neighbour read, roughly, in sectors (order of magnitude: 1, 1,000 or 100,000)?

hints: The neighbouring warp loaded the same sector moments ago.
problems.solution: (a) 20 + 4 = 24. (b) 4 + 4 = 8. (c) A handful of sectors: the previous lanes or warp just touched it. Tiny reuse distances are what caches handle perfectly, even small ones.
